video.title: How Did Giants Survive The Flood If Everyone Died?

transcript.text: Two men carried it on a pole between them.
One cluster of grapes, too heavy for a single man to lift.
Twelve spies had gone into Canaan.
Twelve came back.
And ten of them stood before the whole nation of Israel and said something that should have been impossible.
We saw the Nephilim there.
The Nephilim belong to Genesis 6, to the world before the flood.
Genesis 7 says everything with the breath of life on dry land died in that water.
Eight people walked off the ark.
Eight.
So, how were the Nephilim standing in Canaan?
Either the spies were lying, or the flood missed someone, or something came back.
The Bible gives three clues: a short phrase in Genesis 6, an iron bed, and a city called Gath.
Follow them in order, and the answer turns out to be stranger than the giants.
Numbers 13.
Israel has crossed a desert and watched a sea split.
The promised land lies ahead, and 12 leaders, one from each tribe, spend 40 days inside it.
They return and drop the fruit on the ground.
For a moment, the camp celebrates milk, honey, grapes you can barely carry.
Then the spokesman say one word.
But.
The people are strong.
The cities are fortified and enormous.
In Hebron, they named three men: Ahiman, Shishai, and Talmai, sons of Anak.
Numbers even notes that Hebron was built 7 years before Zoan in Egypt.
These families were old and rooted, and they were not going anywhere.
Then comes the line that has echoed for 35 centuries.
We seem like grasshoppers in our own eyes, and we look the same to them.
The spies had never asked the giants what they thought.
They invented that part.
Scripture's own label for the whole speech is a bad report.
Hold on to that phrase.
The camp wailed until morning.
Numbers 14 says the people talked about choosing a new leader and marching back to Egypt.
A nation that had watched God break an empire was ready to return to slavery.
Only two men stood against it.
Joshua and Caleb tore their clothes and said the land was good and the Lord was with them.
The crowd reached for stones.
Fear like that does not stay on the surface.
It gets into how a person prays and how they stand when something looms larger than they are.
The spies did not say big men.
They chose a word that already had a history: Nephilim.
And that word had appeared in only one place before, Genesis 6, the chapter right before the world drowned.
Genesis 6:4.
The Nephilim were on the earth in those days, and also afterward, when the sons of God went into the daughters of men.
Their children were the mighty men of old, men of renown.
Two details in that verse are usually missed.
First, Genesis 6 never says giants.
It says mighty.
It says renowned.
The Hebrew word itself is debated, and many take it to mean fallen ones.
The picture of towering giants comes later, from the Greek translation called the Septuagint, made centuries afterward, which rendered the word as gigantes.
The idea of size arrived through translation and through frightened spies.
Second, the phrase "and also afterward"—afterward is the word that makes the whole problem.
Set it beside Genesis 7:21-23.
Every creature that moved on the earth perished.
Only Noah and those with him remained.
First Peter 3:20 counts them eight persons.
The text carves out no exception.
So the Bible seems to say two things at once.
Genesis 6 hints the Nephilim continued.
Genesis 7 says the world was wiped clean.
And Numbers 13 says someone at Hebron carried the old name.
Nothing in scripture resolves that in one verse.

transcript.text: which speak of angels who sinned, and second Peter connects that to the flood.
An ancient Jewish text, the Book of Enoch, tells this story at length.
Enoch is tradition, not scripture.
Jude quotes it once, but no church has ever received it as canon.
Opponents answer with Jesus in Matthew 22:30, who says angels do not marry.
The third view says the sons of God were kings, rulers who took wives by force and claimed divine authority.
Now, watch what happens when you apply each one to our question.
If the Nephilim were a human line, nothing stops that strength from continuing through Noah's descendants.
Genesis 10 traces the peoples of Canaan to Noah's grandson.
If they came from an angelic event, some read and also afterward as a repeat.
That is inference.
Scripture never narrates a second descent.
And if Nephilim was simply Israel's word for terrifying strong men, the spies were not reporting flood survivors at all.
They were reaching for the scariest label they knew.
Scripture does not say which is right.
What it does say changes the picture completely because it tells us who the people at Hebron actually were.
Joshua 15:13, Anak was the son of Arba, and Arba founded the city that became Hebron.
Anak had a father, the Anakim had a family tree.
These were not ghosts from before the flood.
They were a people with ancestors.
Deuteronomy adds more names.
The Emim, a great people, tall as the Anakin, the Zamzummim named by the Ammonites.
Each time, Moses ends the same way, the Lord destroyed them, and another nation took their land.
Then Deuteronomy 3:11, a verse that reads like a dare.
Og, King of Bashan, was the last of the Rephaim.
His bed was iron, nine cubits long and four wide, roughly 13 ft by six.
Some scholars debate whether it was a bed or a sarcophagus, but notice where Moses says it sits, in Raba of the Ammonites, as if to say, go and see for yourself.
Last, the Bible is counting them.
Amos 2:9 gives a haunting image.
God says he destroyed the Amorite, tall as cedars, strong as oaks, cutting off the fruit above and the roots beneath.
And Genesis 15:16 shows this was no sudden act.
God told Abraham that judgment would wait four generations because the Amorite's guilt was not yet complete.
The verdict was scheduled centuries ahead.
Now, Joshua 11:21 and 22, Joshua clears the Anakin from Hebron, from Debir, from Anab.
None remain in Israel's land.
Only in Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod do some survive.
Three cities hold that because Hebron was not finished.
Joshua 14 finds Caleb at 85, 45 years after Kadesh.
Every man who wept that night is dead.
Caleb walks up to Joshua and asks for the mountain that broke a nation.
He admits the sons of Anak are there.
Their city is great and fortified.
Then he says four words of stunning humility, perhaps the Lord will be with me.
Joshua 15:14 records what followed.
He drove out Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai, the same three names that made Israel weep.
Now they read like a footnote.
Now, Gath.
Centuries later, in 1 Samuel 17, a champion steps from the Philistine lines, Goliath of Gath, one of the three refugees Joshua named.
Scholars disagree on his height.
The traditional Hebrew text says six cubits in a span, nearly 10 ft.
The Dead Sea Scrolls and the Septuagint read four cubits in a span, about 6 ft 9.
Either way, he froze an army.
He came out morning and evening for 40 days, 40 days, the same number the spies spent in Canaan.
Whether by design or echo, Israel was standing in the same fear a second time.
Then a shepherd boy asked who this uncircumcised Philistine was to defy the armies of the living God.
